name: Perfect VC Pitch Rubric
sources: A review of 23 early-stage startup pitch decks from an MBA entrepreneurship course
Common venture-capital pitch deck frameworks (purpose, problem, solution, market, why now, competition, product, business model, team, financials, ask)
A score-times-confidence approach to startup concept assessment

levels.1: Mentioned: named in passing, no substance
levels.2: Partial: covered, but asserted without evidence or missing key parts
levels.3: Solid: covered well with some evidence; one part thin
levels.4: Investor-grade: complete, specific, backed by data or named evidence

scale.evidence_cap: A criterion whose claims rest only on assertion (no numbers, sources, named customers, interviews or documents) cannot score above level 2.

criteria.name: Company purpose (the hook)
perfect: One declarative sentence says what the company does, for whom, and the outcome
Stated in the first 30 seconds; a listener could repeat it
A memorable framing (an 'X for Y' analogy) is a plus
common_gaps: Opens with team or industry stats before saying what the company is
Mission-speak instead of a concrete sentence

criteria.name: Problem
perfect: A specific customer with a specific pain, quantified (time, money, risk)
How the customer solves it today and why that workaround fails
Who pays for the problem, if different from who feels it
common_gaps: Generic pain ('X is hard') with no numbers

criteria.name: Solution and how it works
perfect: Value proposition tied point-by-point to the problem
How it works: concept flow, product walkthrough or demo
A concrete use case or customer story showing life before and after
common_gaps: Feature list with no link back to the pain
No explanation of how the product is delivered

criteria.name: Customer validation and traction
perfect: Number of customer interviews or surveys stated (e.g. '30 interviews + 120 surveys')
Named or role-attributed customer quotes that confirm the pain and willingness to pay
Hard commitments: LOIs, pilots, pre-orders, waitlist, revenue, grants or partners
What the team learned or changed because of the feedback
common_gaps: 'People love it' with no count or source

criteria.name: Market size and target customer
perfect: TAM top-down, SAM and SOM bottom-up, with sources and the arithmetic shown
A defined beachhead (geography or segment) and why it was chosen
A target customer persona with demographics, behaviours and buying patterns
common_gaps: Huge top-down TAM with no bottom-up SOM

criteria.name: Why now (market drivers)
perfect: Two or more sourced trends (regulatory, technology, demographic, behaviour) that make the timing right
Explains why this was not possible or needed five years ago
common_gaps: Industry growth rate quoted as the only driver

criteria.name: Competition and defensible advantage
perfect: Named direct and indirect competitors, including the status quo
An honest comparison (not a grid where the startup wins every row)
A durable advantage: IP, data, network effects, exclusive partners, cost or switching costs
Answers 'what stops a big player copying this?'
common_gaps: Differentiators that are easy to copy (better UX, local)

criteria.name: Business model and unit economics
perfect: Who pays, how much, how often; every revenue stream named with its relative size
Pricing validated by customers or comparables
Unit economics worked through: price, cost per unit, contribution or gross margin
Customer acquisition cost and lifetime value (or payback period)
common_gaps: Several revenue streams with no sense of which matters

criteria.name: Go-to-market, launch and growth plan
perfect: Channels and message mapped to the funnel (awareness, interest, desire, action)
Launch plan: where you start, first 90 days, first customers
Sales motion and adoption pace (customers per month or quarter)
Growth plan over 36 months with milestones and expansion markets
common_gaps: 'Social media and word of mouth' with no numbers

criteria.name: Team and advisors
perfect: Each founder's role plus the specific experience that makes them able to execute
Advisors or board who fill named gaps (industry, regulatory, technical)
Admits open roles and the plan to fill them
common_gaps: Advisors listed without saying what they add

criteria.name: Financials and assumptions
perfect: 3-year projection: revenue, costs, net income, cash flow
Key assumptions stated and sourced (conversion, retention, price, CAC)
Break-even point (month/quarter and units) and startup costs
Sensitivity or downside case; numbers consistent across the pitch
common_gaps: Numbers that contradict each other (price, margin)

criteria.name: The ask, use of funds and investor return
perfect: Exact amount raised and instrument or terms offered
Use of funds broken down, and the milestone it reaches (break-even or next round)
How investors get a return: exit paths with likely acquirers or comparables

criteria.name: Delivery and storytelling
perfect: Clear narrative arc: hook, problem, solution, proof, plan, ask, strong close
Fits about 10 minutes (roughly 1,200-1,600 spoken words)
Plain language, confident tone, no filler; numbers stated precisely
Hand-offs between presenters are smooth (if a team pitch)
common_gaps: Ends without a call to action

not_scored_from_transcript: Slide design and visuals: not visible in a transcript
Live presence and Q&A: judged in the room, not from text
